blocks.text:
Design the core scoring engine behind a live cricket score and commentary platform like Cricinfo: a scorer records what happens on every single ball bowled, and the platform continuously shows the current score, wickets, overs, and which batsman is on strike. The distinguishing idea is that nothing about the current match state is stored directly. Every delivery is appended to an immutable, ordered log, and the total runs, wickets, overs completed, and strike rotation are all derived by replaying that log from the start of the innings.

  • Actors: Scorer (records each delivery), MatchService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: ball-by-ball delivery recording, legal-versus-extra delivery handling, and state derivation for a single innings.

This is the first event-sourcing style design in this problem set: instead of mutating a running score directly, every action is appended to a log, and the current state is always a pure function of replaying that log, the same pattern real scoring systems use so a full ball-by-ball history is never lost.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Record a delivery: a scorer logs the runs scored, the delivery type (normal, wide, no-ball), and whether a wicket fell on that ball.
Derive current state: at any point, compute the total runs, wickets, overs completed, balls bowled in the current over, and which batsman is on strike.
Distinguish legal from extra deliveries: wides and no-balls add runs but do not count toward the six legal balls that make up an over.
Enforce an overs limit: once an innings reaches its configured overs limit, no further deliveries can be recorded.
Notify on key events: a wicket falling, an over completing, and the innings completing are all events other parts of a real platform would react to.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many concurrent matches and innings must not require touching existing recording logic.
Extensibility: new scoring rules (a different extras convention) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: scoring rules, notification, and delivery id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: deriving the current state is O(deliveries recorded so far), which stays small for a single innings.
Thread safety: two deliveries recorded for the same innings concurrently must not corrupt the event log's order.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should byes and leg-byes be modeled as their own delivery types, or is the scope limited to normal deliveries, wides, and no-balls?
Does a no-ball also grant a free hit on the following delivery, or is that out of scope?
Should the derived state be recomputed fresh on every request, or cached and incrementally updated for performance at very high query volume?
Can a delivery be corrected or removed after being recorded, given the append-only log model?
Should strike rotation account for runs actually run on extras (wides, no-balls), or is that simplified away?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Delivery types are limited to NORMAL, WIDE, and NO_BALL; byes and leg-byes are noted as a future extension, not implemented.

A wide or no-ball always adds exactly 1 extra run and never counts toward the six legal balls of an over; runs scored on an extra delivery are also possible (a batsman can still run) but are folded into the total without affecting strike rotation, a deliberate simplification called out explicitly here.
Strike rotation on a legal, normal delivery follows the standard cricket rule: an odd number of runs rotates strike, an even number does not, and the end of every completed over also rotates strike.
The delivery log is append-only in this design; correcting a mis-recorded delivery is noted as a future improvement, not implemented.
Each innings has a configurable overs limit; once reached, no further deliveries can be recorded for that innings.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Match, Innings, Delivery, DeliveryType, and a derived Match State

items: Match: a top-level contest between two teams, containing one or more innings.
Innings: owns the append-only log of deliveries for one team's batting turn.
Delivery: a single, immutable event describing one ball bowled: runs scored, delivery type, and whether a wicket fell.
MatchState: not a stored entity but a computed value, derived fresh by replaying an innings's delivery log.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A match contains many innings; an innings logs many deliveries in append-only order; state is derived from that log

items: Match to Innings is one-to-many.
Innings to Delivery is one-to-many and strictly ordered, appended in the sequence balls were actually bowled.
Innings to MatchState is a derivation, not a stored relationship: the state is recomputed from the delivery log, not persisted independently of it.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep scoring rules, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: which delivery types count as a legal ball, and how many extra runs each earns, is a rules decision that could plausibly vary (a different tournament format experimenting with different extras conventions) independently of how the delivery log itself is stored and replayed.

metadata.alt: ScoringRuleStrategy interface with StandardScoringRuleStrategy defining legal-ball and extra-run rules per delivery type

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new rules variant is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to MatchService. What it solves: it isolates a rules decision that could change per format from the stable log-replay mechanics.
Why needed: a wicket falling, an over completing, and an innings completing are exactly the moments a real live-scoring platform pushes an update to millions of watching fans.

metadata.alt: MatchObserver interface notified by MatchService on every key scoring event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: MatchService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core recording workflow from side effects like push notifications and commentary updates.
Why needed: delivery id generation should not be scattered across calling code.
Why it is the best fit: every delivery is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Delivery: attributes deliveryId, runsScored, deliveryType, isWicket; responsibility: represent one immutable event.
DeliveryFactory: method createDelivery(runs, type, isWicket); responsibility: generate sequential delivery ids.
Innings: attributes inningsId, battingTeam, bowlingTeam, deliveries, complete; responsibility: own the append-only event log for one batting turn.
MatchState: a plain computed result object; responsibility: represent the derived totals at a point in time.
MatchService: the orchestrator; responsibility: append deliveries, enforce the overs limit, derive state by replay, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: ScoringRuleStrategy and MatchObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: ScoringRuleStrategy: isLegalDelivery(type) and extraRuns(type): abstract away exactly which deliveries count toward an over and how many extras they earn.
MatchObserver: onDeliveryRecorded / onWicketFallen / onOverCompleted / onInningsCompleted: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: The end-to-end recording workflow, alongside its rejection branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Record a delivery, reject if the innings is already complete, append to the log, replay to derive state, and mark complete once the overs limit is hit

items: Happy path: record delivery → innings not yet complete → append to log → replay entire log → return updated state.
Completion path: record delivery → this delivery brings legal ball count to the overs limit → mark innings complete → notify.
Rejection path: record delivery → innings already marked complete → rejected.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: recordDelivery(inningsId, runsScored, deliveryType, isWicket): appends a delivery event and returns the freshly derived match state, or throws if the innings is already complete.
getCurrentState(inningsId): replays the delivery log and returns the current derived state without recording anything new.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: InningsCompleteException: a delivery is recorded after the overs limit has already been reached.
InvalidDeliveryException: a negative runs value or other malformed delivery input.
InvalidInningsException: an unknown innings id.

blocks.text: The critical race is two attempts to record the next delivery for the same innings at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to record the next delivery for the same innings; synchronization ensures the log stays in a single, consistent order

blocks.text: Synchronizing the append-and-derive step per innings ensures deliveries are always appended in a single, well-defined order, which matters enormously here since the entire derived state depends on replaying the log in exactly the order balls were actually bowled.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new scoring rules variant (a tournament experimenting with different extras conventions) is a new ScoringRuleStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (push notifications, live commentary feed) is a new MatchObserver implementation.
Adding byes and leg-byes as new delivery types only requires extending the enum and the strategy's rules, not restructuring the log or replay mechanism.
Caching the derived state and updating it incrementally per delivery, rather than replaying the full log every time, is a natural performance optimization that does not change the public API at all.
Single Responsibility: Innings owns the log, ScoringRuleStrategy decides legality and extras, MatchObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new scoring rules or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to MatchService.
Liskov Substitution: any ScoringRuleStrategy or MatchObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: MatchObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: MatchService depends on the ScoringRuleStrategy and MatchObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A wide or no-ball with a wicket still needs to increment the wicket count, even though it does not count as a legal ball.
The very last legal ball of the overs limit still needs to correctly mark the innings complete in the same operation that records it.
An innings with zero deliveries recorded yet returns a valid, zeroed-out state rather than an error.
Two consecutive extras (a wide followed immediately by a no-ball) correctly add up their extra runs without either counting toward the over.
recordDelivery: O(1) to append, plus O(n) to replay the log and derive fresh state, where n is deliveries recorded so far in the innings.
getCurrentState: O(n) for the same replay.
Space: O(deliveries per innings) held in memory, growing by exactly one entry per ball bowled.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

items: Delivery rows are strictly append-only and ordered by a sequenceNumber column, never updated or deleted, matching the event-sourcing model directly.
An index on Delivery(inningsId, sequenceNumber) supports fast, in-order replay of a single innings's log.
Cache the derived state and update it incrementally per delivery instead of replaying the full log on every request, once innings length makes full replay noticeably slow.
Add byes and leg-byes as additional delivery types.
Support correcting a mis-recorded delivery by appending a compensating correction event, rather than mutating the log, preserving the append-only guarantee.
Model a free hit following a no-ball, where a wicket cannot be given except for a run out.

items: Why replay the entire log instead of maintaining a running total incrementally? Replaying from scratch guarantees the derived state can never drift out of sync with the actual sequence of events, at the cost of O(n) work per query; a production system would likely cache the last computed state and apply just the newest delivery incrementally, falling back to a full replay only when rebuilding from scratch (for example after a crash).

Why does a wide or no-ball still increment the wicket count even though it does not count as a legal ball? Because a batsman can still be run out or stumped on an illegal delivery in real cricket, so wicket-taking and over-progress are genuinely independent concerns in the rules.

How would you extend this to support byes and leg-byes? Add them as new DeliveryType values and extend the strategy's extraRuns and isLegalDelivery methods, without touching the replay loop's structure at all.

Full log replay vs incrementally maintained state: full replay is simple and always correct by construction, at the cost of O(n) work per state query; incremental maintenance is faster per query but introduces the risk of the maintained state silently drifting from what the log actually says if an update is ever missed.

Append-only log vs mutable score fields: the append-only log preserves a complete, auditable ball-by-ball history for free (useful for full scorecards, replays, and dispute resolution), at the cost of more storage and computation than simply mutating a running total directly.

Simplified extras (no strike rotation on wides or no-balls) vs full real-world rules: the simplification keeps the derivation logic easy to reason about and test, at the cost of not perfectly matching every real cricket scoring nuance, which a production scorer would need to layer on top.
Persist the delivery log in an append-only table in a real database, using the schema in the Database Design section, rather than an in-memory list.

Emit delivery, wicket, over-completed, and innings-completed events to a message queue so downstream systems (live commentary, push notifications, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Cache the derived state after each delivery and update it incrementally rather than replaying the full log on every single read, once innings length makes full replay noticeably slow.
Expose metrics on replay latency per innings, which would reveal exactly when the incremental-caching optimization becomes worth the added complexity.
